newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - A.H. Belo acquisition gives more balance.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - A.H. Belo acquisition gives more balance.

text.p: A.H. Belo Corp 's acquisition of Providence Journal Co will give it a better geographical and network balance in broadcasting and a firm spot in the strong Seattle market, Chief Financial Officer Michael Perry said.
Perry said the acqusition was mainly aimed at boosting Belo's broadcast holdings and that its seven television stations fit well with the Providence Journal's nine stations.
"It gives us a geographic balance in very high growth areas and also gives us a balance among the networks," he told Reuters in a telephone interview.

The $1.5 billion buy-out combines Belo's seven network-affiliated stations -- three CBS, three ABC, and one UPN -- with Providence Journal's portfolio of five NBC affiliates, two Fox, one ABC and one CBS.
Belo's audience reach, which will grow from 8 percent to 12.3 percent, will be equally balanced among the big three networks, Perry said, adding that other buyouts were possible.
"We have been looking for more stations and would not rule out that possibility. On a proforma basis, the company still has a pretty strong balance sheet and has capacity for further acquisitions."

Of Providence Journal's stations, Belo is most excited about KING-TV, the NBC affiliate in Seattle. "In terms of demographics and growth profile, it is a very good market with a tremendous amount of immigration to the market," Perry said.
Control of KING-TV will force Belo to divest of its own KIRO-TV, a UPN affiliate, in Seattle.
Perry said Belo has already received offers priced at well above what it paid for KIRO-TV but did not necessarily want a straight sale.
"What we'd love to do is trade that station for one of the more strategically important stations elsewhere and broaden the broadcast portfolio," he said.

The Providence Journal has the right to operate another Seattle station under a local management agreement, and also owns NorthWest Cable News, a regional 24-hour cable channel available in about 1.4 million homes in the Pacific Northwest.

Perry said the acquisition would probably not carry any sizeable one-off charge and that the combined company would give Belo greater bargaining power to buy news print and broadcast programming at cheaper rates.
He said the acquisition will be "quite dilutive" to earnings per share primarily because of the amortization of $1.2 billion in goodwill resulting from the deal.
But Perry said cash flow per share, which is "far less diluted", would be a more accurate way of tracking performance going forward.

Under the acqusition deal, which must still be approved by shareholders and the Federal Communications Commission to transfer station licenses, Providence Journal shareholders would receive $12.33 in cash and 0.5333 shares of Belo series A common stock for each share of Providence Journal.
Perry said he expects the deal to be approved and finalized in the first half of 1997.
While the rationale behind the acquisition was focused on the broadcast side, Perry insisted the newspaper publishing side of the alliance would not be neglected.
"At the core of our business is the Dallas Morning News, at the core of theirs is the Providence Journal-Bulletin. And that is an important part of this merger as well," he said.
